dataset_metadata.disclaimer: New AI-generated English drafts of the recorded Classical Chinese; not scholarly reviewed. Original source interpretations are not verified geometry or modern etymology.

shuowen:501.text: Yellow flowers. Formed from 艸, with 黊 indicating the sound. Pronounced like 壞.

shuowen:502.text: The yellow flowers of 苕. Formed from 艸, with 𤐫 indicating the sound. Another explanation: the tip.

shuowen:503.text: A plant that flowers but does not bear fruit. Another explanation: yellow blossoms. Formed from 艸, with 央 indicating the sound.

shuowen:504.text: Abundant flowers. Formed from 艸, with 爾 indicating the sound. The Odes says: “What is that flourishing thing？”

shuowen:505.text: Luxuriant plants. Formed from 艸, with 妻 indicating the sound. The Odes says: “Lush and luxuriant.”

shuowen:506.text: Luxuriant plants. Formed from 艸, with 奉 indicating the sound.

shuowen:507.text: Luxuriant. Formed from 艸, with 疑 indicating the sound. The Odes says: “Millets grow luxuriantly.”

shuowen:508.text: The appearance of flowers hanging from plants and trees. Formed from 艸, with 甤 indicating the sound.

shuowen:509.text: In Qing, Qi, Yan and Ji, fine tree branches are called 葼. Formed from 艸, with 㚇 indicating the sound.

shuowen:510.text: Plants wilting and drooping. Formed from 艸, with 移 indicating the sound.

shuowen:511.text: The form of plants and trees. Formed from 艸, with 原 indicating the sound.

shuowen:512.text: Plant fruit or seed pods. Formed from 艸, with 夾 indicating the sound.

shuowen:513.text: The tip of a plant. Formed from 艸, with 亾 indicating the sound.

shuowen:514.text: The flowering head of 藍蓼. Formed from 艸, with abbreviated 隨 indicating the sound.

shuowen:515.text: The attachment of a melon. Formed from 艸, with 帶 indicating the sound.

shuowen:516.text: Plant roots. Formed from 艸, with 亥 indicating the sound.

shuowen:517.text: Roots, 茇; the roots of 茅 grass. Formed from 艸, with 均 indicating the sound.

shuowen:518.text: Plant roots. Formed from 艸, with 犮 indicating the sound. In spring, pulling dry plant roots lifts the soil, called 撥; hence they are called 茇. Another explanation calls a plant's white flowers 茇.

shuowen:519.text: Luxuriant plants. Formed from 艸, with 凡 indicating the sound. The Odes says: “Luxuriant millet seedlings.”

shuowen:520.text: Flowers and leaves spreading out. Formed from 艸, with 傅 indicating the sound. Pronounced like 傅.

shuowen:521.text: Plants and trees failing to grow. Another explanation: 茅 grass shoots. Formed from 艸, with 執 indicating the sound.

shuowen:522.text: The appearance of abundant plants. Formed from 艸, with 㹞 indicating the sound. Pingchun in Jiangxia has a 䓄 station.

shuowen:523.text: Plants growing abundantly and luxuriantly. Formed from 艸, with 戊 indicating the sound.

shuowen:524.text: Luxuriant plants. Formed from 艸, with 畼 indicating the sound.

shuowen:525.text: Ground shaded by plants. Formed from 艸, with 陰 indicating the sound.

shuowen:526.text: The appearance of plants. Formed from 艸, with 造 indicating the sound.

shuowen:527.text: Plants and trees increasing in abundance. Formed from 艸, with abbreviated 兹 indicating the sound.

shuowen:528.text: Plants completely withered by drought. Formed from 艸, with 俶 indicating the sound. The Odes says: “Parched are the mountains and rivers.”

shuowen:529.text: The appearance of plants. Formed from 艸, with 歊 indicating the sound. The Rites of Zhou says: “The hub is worn but does not warp.”

shuowen:530.text: The appearance of abundant plants. Formed from 艸, with 旣 indicating the sound.

shuowen:531.text: The appearance of abundant plants. Formed from 艸, with 資 indicating the sound.

shuowen:532.text: The appearance of luxuriant plants. Formed from 艸, with 秦 indicating the sound.

shuowen:533.text: The appearance of noxious weeds. Formed from 艸, with 肖 indicating the sound.

shuowen:534.text: 芮芮: the appearance of plants growing. Formed from 艸, with 内 indicating the sound. Pronounced like 汭.

shuowen:535.text: The appearance of plants. Formed from 艸, with 在 indicating the sound. Jibei has Chiping county.

shuowen:536.text: The appearance of abundant plants. Formed from 艸, with 會 indicating the sound. The Odes says: “Thickly gathered and luxuriant.”

shuowen:537.text: Fine grasses growing in clumps. Formed from 艸, with 敄 indicating the sound.

shuowen:538.text: Plants covering and spreading. Formed from 艸, with 毛 indicating the sound. The Odes says: “Gather it to left and right.”

shuowen:539.text: The color of plants. Formed from 艸, with 倉 indicating the sound.

shuowen:540.text: The appearance of plants receiving the wind. Formed from 艸 and 風. Pronounced like 婪.

shuowen:541.text: The appearance of plants. Formed from 艸, with 卒 indicating the sound. Pronounced like 瘁.

shuowen:542.text: To transplant separately. Formed from 艸, with 時 indicating the sound.

shuowen:543.text: Plants growing in a field. Formed from 艸 and 田.

shuowen:544.text: Small plants. Formed from 艸, with 可 indicating the sound.

shuowen:545.text: Weedy overgrowth, 薉. Formed from 艸, with 無 indicating the sound.

shuowen:546.text: Weedy overgrowth, 蕪. Formed from 艸, with 歲 indicating the sound.

shuowen:547.text: Weedy overgrowth. Formed from 艸, with 㠩 indicating the sound. Another explanation: plants covering the ground.

shuowen:548.text: Plants in disorder. Formed from 艸, with 寍 indicating the sound. Du Lin explains: the tangled appearance of plants, 𦱊𦺝.

shuowen:549.text: The tangled appearance called 𦱊𦺝. Formed from 艸, with 爭 indicating the sound.

shuowen:550.text: For herbaceous plants, falling is called 零; for trees, 落. Formed from 艸, with 洛 indicating the sound.

shuowen:551.text: 蔽蔽: small plants. Formed from 艸, with 敝 indicating the sound.

shuowen:552.text: Bark and leaves of plants and trees fallen to the ground are called 蘀. Formed from 艸, with 擇 indicating the sound. The Odes says: “In the tenth month leaves fall.”

shuowen:553.text: To accumulate. Formed from 艸, with 温 indicating the sound. The Spring and Autumn commentary says: “Accumulating profit produces evil.”

shuowen:554.text: Withered, 菸. Formed from 艸, with 焉 indicating the sound.

shuowen:555.text: Stifled or withered. Formed from 艸, with 於 indicating the sound. Another explanation: wilted, 𣨙.

shuowen:556.text: The appearance of plants winding around. Formed from 艸, with 榮 indicating the sound. The Odes says: “Kudzu vines wind around it.”

shuowen:557.text: A plant. Formed from 艸, with 祭 indicating the sound.

shuowen:558.text: Plants with many leaves. Formed from 艸, with 伐 indicating the sound. The Spring and Autumn commentary says: “Di Fa of Jin.”

shuowen:559.text: Edible plants. Formed from 艸, with 采 indicating the sound.

shuowen:560.text: The appearance of plants with many leaves. Formed from 艸, with 而 indicating the sound. Chengfu in Pei has a Yanger station.

shuowen:561.text: The appearance of plants floating in water. Formed from 艸, with 乏 indicating the sound.

shuowen:562.text: A wooded thicket. Another explanation: a silkworm tray. Formed from 艸, with 溥 indicating the sound.

shuowen:563.text: A place for rearing birds and beasts. Formed from 艸, with 夗 indicating the sound.

shuowen:564.text: A great marsh. Formed from 艸, with 𢿙 indicating the sound. The marshes of the nine provinces are: Juqu in Yangzhou, Yunmeng in Jingzhou, Futian in Yuzhou, Mengzhu in Qingzhou, Daye in Yanzhou, Xianpu in Yongzhou, Xiyang in Youzhou, Yangyu in Jizhou, and Zhaoyuqi in Bingzhou.

shuowen:565.text: Uncultivated land. Formed from 艸 and 甾. The Changes says: “Without clearing new fields or cultivating old ones.”

shuowen:566.text: The appearance of luxuriant plants. Formed from 艸, with 繇 indicating the sound. The Book of Xia says: “Its plants were luxuriant.”

shuowen:567.text: To remove plants. The Bright Hall Monthly Ordinances says: “In late summer burn the cut vegetation.” Formed from 艸, with 雉 indicating the sound.

shuowen:568.text: To plow ground thick with plants. Formed from 艸 and 耒; 耒 also indicates the sound.

shuowen:569.text: Large plants. Formed from 艸, with 致 indicating the sound.

shuowen:570.text: Plants growing together in enclosing clusters. Formed from 艸, with 斬 indicating the sound. The Documents says: “Plants and trees grow in clusters.” [The precise sense of 蔪苞 is uncertain.]

shuowen:571.text: A road so overgrown with plants that it cannot be traveled. Formed from 艸, with 弗 indicating the sound.

shuowen:572.text: Fragrant. Formed from 艸, with 必 indicating the sound.

shuowen:573.text: A fragrant plant. Formed from 艸, with 設 indicating the sound.

shuowen:574.text: A fragrant plant. Formed from 艸, with 方 indicating the sound.

shuowen:575.text: Mixed fragrant plants. Formed from 艸, with 賁 indicating the sound.

shuowen:576.text: Plants for treating illness. Formed from 艸, with 樂 indicating the sound.

shuowen:577.text: Plants and trees growing attached to the soil. Formed from 艸, with 麗 indicating the sound. The Changes says: “The hundred grains, plants and trees cling to the earth.”

shuowen:578.text: Broad and abundant. Formed from 艸, with 席 indicating the sound.

shuowen:579.text: To cut plants. Formed from 艸 and 殳.

shuowen:580.text: A mat or bedding. Formed from 艸, with 存 indicating the sound.

shuowen:581.text: Bedding for a sacrifice. Another explanation: unplaited plants lying scattered. Formed from 艸, with 耤 indicating the sound.

shuowen:582.text: A bedding of white grass. Formed from 艸, with 租 indicating the sound. The Rites says: “Enfeoff lords with earth, bedding it in white 茅 grass.”

shuowen:583.text: At court assemblies, bundles of 茅 marking positions are called 蕝. Formed from 艸, with 絕 indicating the sound. The Spring and Autumn Discourses of the States says: “Set out reed bundles to mark the seats.”

shuowen:584.text: To roof a house with grass and reeds. Formed from 艸, with 次 indicating the sound.

shuowen:585.text: To thatch, 茨. Formed from 艸, with 咠 indicating the sound.

shuowen:586.text: A thatch covering. Formed from 艸, with 盇 indicating the sound.

shuowen:587.text: A covering. Formed from 艸, with 占 indicating the sound.

shuowen:588.text: A covering. Formed from 艸, with 渴 indicating the sound.

shuowen:589.text: A brush. Formed from 艸, with 屈 indicating the sound.

shuowen:590.text: A screen or barrier. Formed from 艸, with 潘 indicating the sound.

shuowen:591.text: Pickled vegetables. Formed from 艸, with 沮 indicating the sound.

shuowen:592.text: Crisp pickled mustard. Formed from 艸, with 全 indicating the sound.

shuowen:593.text: Preserved chives. Formed from 艸, with 酤 indicating the sound.

shuowen:594.text: Pickled melon. Formed from 艸, with 監 indicating the sound.

shuowen:595.text: Pickled vegetables. Formed from 艸, with 泜 indicating the sound.

shuowen:596.text: A kind of dried plum. Formed from 艸, with 橑 indicating the sound. The Rites of Zhou says: “The bamboo baskets for food offerings contain dried 䕩.” In the Later Han, the king of Changsha first boiled plants to make 䕩.

shuowen:597.text: Boiled-down 茱萸. Formed from 艸, with 𩕺 indicating the sound. Han regulations: Kuaiji presents one peck of 𧆈.

shuowen:598.text: Vegetables for soup. Formed from 艸, with 宰 indicating the sound.

shuowen:599.text: To select vegetables. Formed from 艸 and 右; 右 is a hand. Another explanation: 杜若, a fragrant plant.

shuowen:600.text: A clump of 蒲 reeds. Formed from 艸, with 專 indicating the sound.
